01 / The question

What happens when retrieved social-web content tries to become an instruction?

Why this matters

Retrieval-augmented generation can give language models useful context, but it also brings untrusted text into the answer pipeline. Hidden-in-Plain-Text introduces OpenRAG-Soc to evaluate indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning in that setting.

02 / Contribution & method

A joint contribution

I coauthored OpenRAG-Soc, a benchmark and evaluation harness for social-web prompt injection in RAG.

Role & scope

I coauthored this work with Ziqi Wei. The joint contribution is a benchmark and evaluation harness for comparing web-native attack carriers, retrievers, and mitigations. The public materials do not specify an individual implementation split, so the system contributions below are attributed to the joint work.

01Vary retrieval＋

Vary the retrieval path

Pair a social-web corpus with interchangeable sparse and dense retrievers.

02Compare defenses＋

Evaluate mitigations

Compare HTML/Markdown sanitization, Unicode normalization, and attribution-gated answering.

03Measure trade-offs＋

Measure the trade-offs

Track answer-time attacks, retrieval rank shifts, utility, and latency within an end-to-end evaluation.

04 / The next question

How can an agent use retrieved evidence without treating that evidence as authority?

A direction to explore

A useful extension would connect pipeline-level defenses with interfaces that help people inspect attribution and understand when a source has influenced an answer. This is a prospective research direction.
